'''''Palmaria palmata''''', also called '''dulse''', '''dillisk''' or '''dilsk''' (from [[Irish language|Irish]]/[[Scottish Gaelic]] ''{{lang|ga|duileasc}}''/''{{lang|gd|duileasg}}''), '''red dulse''', '''sea lettuce flakes''', or '''creathnach''', is a [[red algae|red alga]] ([[Rhodophyta]]) previously referred to as ''Rhodymenia palmata''. It grows on the northern coasts of the [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic]] and [[Pacific Ocean]]s. It is a well-known snack food. In [[Iceland]], where it is known as ''{{lang|is|söl}}'' {{IPA|is|ˈsœːl̥|}}, it has been an important source of [[dietary fibre]] throughout the centuries.

==History==
5th century laws of [[Ireland#Late antiquity and early medieval times|archaic Ireland]] existed concerning eating ''duileasc''.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Pierrick Stévant|display-authors=et al.|url=https://mnhn.hal.science/mnhn-03932032|title=Concise review of the red macroalga dulse, Palmaria palmata (L.) Weber & Mohr|doi=10.1007/s10811-022-02899-5|journal=[[Journal of Applied Phycology]]|date=2023|quote=[[Bretons|Breton]]" [''sic''] "Rhatigan 2009}}</ref>{{clarify|date=April 2026}}

==Description==
The erect frond of dulse grows attached by its discoid [[holdfast (biology)|holdfast]] and a short inconspicuous [[Stipe (botany)|stipe]] epiphytically on to the stipe of ''[[Laminaria]]'' or to rocks. The [[fronds]] are variable in shape and colour from deep rose to reddish purple and are rather leathery in texture. The flat foliose blade gradually expands and divides into broad segments ranging in size to {{convert|50|cm}} long and {{convert|3|-|8|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} in width which can bear flat, wedge-shaped proliferations from the edge.<ref name="Hoek, Mann and Jahns 95">Hoek, C.van den, Mann, D.G. and Jahns, H.M. 1995. ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=xuUoiFesSHMC Algae: An Introduction to Phycology]''. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge. {{ISBN|0-521-30419-9}}.</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.algaebase.org/search/species/detail/?species_id=1|title=Algaebase|website=algaebase.org}}</ref> The blade consists of an outer cortex of small cells enclosing a medulla of larger cells up to 0.35 thick.<ref>Bunker, F.StP, Brodie, J.A., Maggs, C.A. and Bunker, A.R.2017. ''Seaweeds of Britain and Ireland'' Second edition, Wild Nature Press, Plymouth.UK.{{ISBN|978-0-9955673-3-7}}</ref><ref>Irvine, L.M.1983. ''Seaweeds of the British Isles. Volume 1 Rhodophyta Part 2A'' {{ISBN|0-565-00871-4}}</ref>

The reference to ''Rhodymenia palmata'' var. ''mollis'' in Abbott and Hollenberg (1976),<ref name="Abbott and Hollenberg 76">Abbott, I.A. and Hollenberg, G.J. 1976. ''Marine Algae of California.'' Stanford University Press, California. {{ISBN|0-8047-0867-3}}.</ref> is now considered to refer to a different species: ''[[Palmaria mollis]]'' (Setchel et Gardner) van der Meer et Bird.<ref name="Mondragon and Mondragon 03">Mondragon, J. and Mondragon, J. 2003. ''Seaweeds of the Pacific Coast.'' Sea Challengers, California. {{ISBN|0-930118-29-4}}.</ref><ref name="AlgaeBase15100"/>

Dulse is similar to another [[seaweed]], ''[[Dilsea carnosa]]'',<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.algaebase.org/search/species/detail/?species_id=128|title=Algaebase|website=algaebase.org}}</ref> but ''Dilsea'' is more leathery with blades up to {{convert|30|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|20|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} wide. Unlike ''P. palmata'', it is not branched and does not have proliferations or branches from the edge of the frond, although the older blades may split.<ref name="Hiscock 86">Hiscock, S. 1986. ''A Field Key to the British Red Seaweeds.'' Occasional Publications No. 13. Field Studies Council, Dorset Press, Dorchester {{ISBN|1-85153-813-5}}.</ref>

==Life history==
{{technical|date=October 2016}}
The full haplodiploid life history was not fully explained until 1980.<ref name="van der Merr and Todd 80">{{cite journal |author=John P. van der Meer & Edna R. Todd |year=1980 |title=The life history of ''Palmaria palmata'' in culture. A new type for the Rhodophyta |journal=[[Canadian Journal of Botany]] |volume=58 |issue=11 |pages=1250–1256 |doi=10.1139/b80-155|bibcode=1980CaJB...58.1250V }}</ref> There are two phases in the life-history, with a [[haploid]] phase that is [[dioecious]], with separate male and female plants. The large haploid plants are male, having sporangia. Spermatial sori occur scattered over most of the frond of the haploid male plant. The male plants are blade-like and produce spermatia which fertilize the carpogonia of the female crust. The female [[gametophyte]] is very small stunted or encrusted, the [[Carpogonium|carpogonia]], the female nucleus, apparently occurring as single cells in the young plants. The female plants are minute, less than 1 mm), and  after fertilization become overgrown  by the resulting diploid plant.<ref name ="Bunker 2017">Bunker, F.StP.D., Brodie, J.A., Maggs, C.A. and Bunker A.R. 2017. ''Seaweeds of Britain and Ireland'' Second Edition, Wild Nature press, Plymouth, UK {{ISBN|978-0-9955673-3-7}}</ref> [[Tetraspore]]s occur in scattered patches [[Sorus|sori]] (spores) on the mature [[diploid]] blade. The adult [[tetrasporaphyte|tetrasporophyte]] produces tetraspores [[meiosis|meiotically]] in fours.<ref name="Hoek, Mann and Jahns 95"/><ref name="Irvine 83">Irvine, L.M. & Guiry, M.D. "Palmariales and Rhodymeniales" in Irvine, L.M. 1983. ''Seaweeds of the British Isles. Volume 1. Part 2A. Cryptonemiales (sensu stricto) Palamriales, Rhodymeniales.'' British Museum (Natural History), London. {{ISBN|0-565-00871-4}}</ref>

==Ecology==
''P. palmata'' is to be found growing from mid-tide of the [[intertidal zone]] (the area between the high tide and low tide) to depths of 20 m or more in sheltered and exposed shores.<ref name="Irvine 83"/>

==Culinary use==
{{Cookbook|Dulse}}Dulse is commonly used as food and medicine in [[Ireland]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.seaveg.co.uk/dulse.html|title=Finest quality SeaVeg Irish Dulse, harvested from the clean waters of North West Donegal|website=seaveg.co.uk|access-date=2007-02-08|archive-date=2012-02-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120222192457/http://www.seaveg.co.uk/dulse.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> Iceland and [[Atlantic Canada]]. It can be found in many [[health food]] stores or fish markets and can be ordered directly from local distributors. It is also used as fodder for animals in some countries.

Dulse is a good source of minerals and [[vitamin]]s compared with other [[vegetable]]s, contains all [[trace element]]s needed by humans, and has a high [[protein]] content.<ref name="Indergaard and Minsaas 91a">Indergaard, M. and Minsaas, J. 1991. 2 "Animal and human nutrition." in Guiry, M.D. and Blunden, G. 1991. ''Seaweed Resources in Europe: Uses and Potential.'' John Wiley & Sons. {{ISBN|0-471-92947-6}}</ref> Dulse contains [[iodine]], which prevents [[goitre]].

It is commonly found from June to September and can be picked by hand when the tide is out. When picked, small snails, shell pieces, and other small particles can be washed or shaken off the plant, which is then spread to dry. Some gatherers may turn it once and roll it into large bales to be packaged later.

Fresh dulse can be eaten directly off the rocks before sun-drying. Sun-dried dulse is eaten as is or is ground to flakes or a powder. When used in cooking, dulse's properties are similar to those of a flavour-enhancer. In Iceland, the tradition is to eat it with [[butter]].{{Citation needed|reason=I'm an Icelandic person and I've literally never heard of this.|date=July 2021}}. It can be [[Pan frying|pan-fried]] quickly into chips, baked in the oven covered with [[cheese]], with [[Salsa (sauce)|salsa]], or simply microwaved briefly. It can be used in [[soups]], chowders, sandwiches, and salads, or added to bread or pizza [[dough]]. Finely diced, it can be used as a flavour enhancer in [[meat]] dishes, such as [[Chili con carne|chili]], in place of [[monosodium glutamate]].

In Ireland dulse can be used to make "White Soda Bread".<ref>Allen, R. ''Coast Recipes inspired by Ireland's Wild Atlantic Coast'' p.155 HarperCollins {{ISBN|978-0-00-746243-8}}</ref> In [[Ballycastle, County Antrim|Ballycastle]], Northern Ireland, it is traditionally sold at the [[Ould Lammas Fair]]. It is particularly popular along the [[Giant's Causeway|Causeway Coast]]. Although a fast-dying tradition,{{Citation needed|date=August 2008}} many gather their own dulse. Along the [[Ulster]] coastline from [[County Down]] to [[County Donegal]], it is eaten dried and uncooked as a snack. It is commonly referred to as dillisk on the west coast of Ireland. Dillisk is usually dried and sold as a snack food from stalls in seaside towns by periwinkle sellers.

Researchers at [[Oregon State University]]'s [[Hatfield Marine Science Center]] have selected a fast-growing strain of Pacific dulse (''P. mollis''). Originally intended as a [[Animal feed|feed]] for [[abalone]] farming, they claim their strain of the seaweed tastes like bacon when fried.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://oregonstate.edu/ua/ncs/archives/2015/jul/osu-researchers-discover-unicorn-%E2%80%93-seaweed-tastes-bacon|title=OSU researchers discover the unicorn – seaweed that tastes like bacon! - News & Research Communications - Oregon State University|website=oregonstate.edu|date=2015-07-14}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://time.com/3960421/seaweed-bacon-dulse-kale-super-food/|title=New Seaweed Tastes 'Like Bacon' and Is Healthier Than Kale|author=Helen Regan|magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]]|date=16 July 2015 }}</ref>

==Distribution==
''P. palmata'' is the only species of ''Palmaria'' found on the coast of [[Atlantic]] [[Europe]]. It can be found from [[Portugal]] to the [[Baltic Sea|Baltic]] coasts and on the coasts of Iceland and the [[Faroe Islands]].<ref name="Börgesen 03">[[Frederik Børgesen|Børgesen, F.]] (1903) Marine algæ. In: ''[[Botany of the Faeroes|Botany of the Færöes]]'' Vol. II, pp. 339-532. Copenhagen and London.</ref> It also grows on the shores of Arctic [[Russia]], Arctic Canada, Atlantic Canada, [[Alaska]], [[Japan]], and [[Korea]].<ref name="Irvine 83"/> Records of ''P. palmaria'' from [[California]] are actually of ''Palmaria mollis''.<ref name="AlgaeBase15100">{{cite web|url=https://www.algaebase.org/search/species/detail/?species_id=15100|title=Algaebase|website=algaebase.org}}</ref>

==Parasites and diseases==
[[Gall]]s, possibly produced by parasitic [[nematode]]s, [[copepod]]s or [[bacteria]], are known to infect these plants. They were recorded as "outgrowths of tissue produced by the presence...of an animal."<ref name="Irvine 83"/><ref name="Barton">{{cite journal |author=Ethel Sarel Barton |year=1891 |title=On the occurrence of galls in ''Rhodymenia palmata'' Grev |journal=[[Journal of Botany, British and Foreign]] |volume=29 |pages=65–68 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/109998#page/85/mode/1up}}</ref>
